entries.9e7554c6b9432f405446c27b58d692f18d306d3e: <div sID="gen32117" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Col.4" sID="Col.4"/> <div eID="gen32117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32118" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32119" type="x-p"/> I. He continues his account of the duty of masters, from the close of the former chapter, <reference osisRef="Col.4.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. He exhorts to the duty of prayer (<reference osisRef="Col.4.2-Col.4.4">ver. 2-4</reference>), and to a prudent and decent conduct towards those with whom we converse, <reference osisRef="Col.4.5-Col.4.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. III. He closes the epistle with the mention of several of his friends, of whom he gives an honourable testimony, <reference osisRef="Col.4.7-Col.4.18">ver. 7-18</reference>.
entries.1db0a9dad3a1f4445ec7bc8c836d6760c0dc2b04: <div eID="gen32119" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32118" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Relative Duties. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32120" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Masters, give unto <hi type="italic">your</hi> servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven. <div eID="gen32120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32121" type="x-p"/> The apostle proceeds with the duty of masters to their servants, which might have been joined to the foregoing chapter, and is a part of that discourse. Here observe, 1. Justice is required of them: <hi type="italic">Give unto your servants that which is just and equal</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.4.1">v. 1</reference>), not only strict justice, but equity and kindness. Be faithful to your promises to them, and perform your agreements; not defrauding them of their dues, nor <hi type="italic">keeping back by fraud the hire of the labourers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jam. v. 4</reference>. Require no more of them than they are able to perform; and do not lay unreasonable burdens upon them, and beyond their strength. Provide for them what is fit, supply proper food and physic, and allow them such liberties as may fit them the better for cheerful service and make it the easier to them, and this though they be employed in the meanest and lowest offices, and of another country and a different religion from yourselves. 2. A good reason for this regard: "<hi type="italic">Knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.</hi> You who are masters of others have a Master yourself, and are servants of another Lord. You are not lords of yourselves, and are accountable to one above you. Deal with your servants as you expect God should deal with you, and as those who believe they must give an account. You are both servants of the same Lord in the different relations in which you stand, and are equally accountable to him at last. <hi type="italic">Knowing that your Master also is in heaven, neither is there respect of persons with him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">Eph. vi. 9</reference>.
entries.761309d125e7f3d04890ae6d1f3acc6d99ec9296: <div eID="gen32121" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostolic Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32122" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving; <hi type="super">3</hi> Withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds: <hi type="super">4</hi> That I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak. <div eID="gen32122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32123" type="x-p"/> If this be considered as connected with the foregoing verse, then we may observe that it is part of the duty which masters owe their servants to pray with them, and to pray daily with them, or <hi type="italic">continue in prayer.</hi> They must not only do justly and kindly by them, but act a Christian and religious part, and be concerned for their souls as well as their bodies: "As parts of your charge, and under your influence, be concerned for the blessing of God upon them, as well as the success of your affairs in their hands." And this is the duty of every one—to <hi type="italic">continue in prayer.</hi> "Keep up your constant times of prayer, without being diverted from it by other business; keep your hearts close to the duty, without wandering or deadness, and even to the end of it: <hi type="italic">Watching the same.</hi>" Christians should lay hold of all opportunities for prayer, and choose the fittest seasons, which are least liable to disturbance from other things, and keep their minds lively in the duty, and in suitable frames.—<hi type="italic">With thanksgiving,</hi> or solemn acknowledgment of the mercies received. Thanksgiving must have a part in every prayer.—<hi type="italic">Withal praying also for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.4.3">v. 3</reference>. The people must pray particularly for their ministers, and bear them upon their hearts at all times at the throne of grace. As if he had said, "Do not forget us, whenever you pray for yourselves," <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Eph. vi. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.25">1 Thess. v. 25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">Heb. xiii. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">That God would open to us a door of utterance,</hi> that is, either afford opportunity to preach the gospel (so he says, <hi type="italic">a great door and effectual is opened to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">1 Cor. xvi. 9</reference>), or else give me ability and courage, and enable me with freedom and faithfulness; so <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Eph. vi. 19</reference>, <hi type="italic">And for me, that utterance may be given to me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds;</hi> that is, either the deepest doctrines of the gospel with plainness, of which Christ is the principal subject (he calls it the <hi type="italic">mystery of the gospel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Eph. vi. 19</reference>), or else he means the preaching of the gospel to the Gentile world, which he calls the <hi type="italic">mystery hidden from ages</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.1.26">ch. i. 26</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">mystery of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.3.4">Eph. iii. 4</reference>. For this he was now in bonds. He was a prisoner at Rome, by the violent opposition of the malicious Jews. He would have them pray for him, that he might not be discouraged in his work, nor driven from it by his sufferings: "<hi type="italic">That I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.4.4">v. 4</reference>. That I may make this mystery known to those who have not heard of it, and make it plain to their understanding, in such a manner as I ought to do." He had been particular in telling them what he prayed for on their behalf, <reference osisRef="Col.1.9-Col.1.11">ch. i</reference>. Here he tells them particularly what he would have them pray for on his behalf. Paul knew as well as any man how to speak; and yet he begged their prayers for him, that he might be taught to speak. The best and most eminent Christians need the prayers of meaner Christians, and are not above asking them. The chief speakers need prayer, that God would give them a door of utterance, and that they may speak as they ought to speak.
entries.3b2978ae3c5439d672b634a8fe72987aad63abfd: <div eID="gen32123" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostolic Exhortations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32124" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time. <hi type="super">6</hi> Let your speech <hi type="italic">be</hi> alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man. <div eID="gen32124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32125" type="x-p"/> The apostle exhorts them further to a prudent and decent conduct towards all those with whom they conversed, towards the heathen world, or those out of the Christian church among whom they lived (<reference osisRef="Col.4.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Walk in wisdom towards those who are without.</hi> Be careful, in all your converse with them, to get no hurt by them, or contract any of their customs; for <hi type="italic">evil communications corrupt good manners;</hi> and to do not hurt to them, or increase their prejudices against religion, and give them an occasion of dislike. Yea, do them all the good you can, and by all the fittest means and in the proper seasons recommend religion to them.—<hi type="italic">Redeeming the time;</hi> that is, either "improving every opportunity of doing them good, and making the best use of your time in proper duty" (diligence in redeeming time very much recommends religion to the good opinion of others), or else "walking cautiously and with circumspections, to give them no advantage against you, nor expose yourselves to their malice and ill-will," <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15-Eph.5.16">Eph. v. 15, 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Walk circumspectly, redeeming the time, because the days are evil,</hi> that is, dangerous, or times of trouble and suffering. And towards others, or those who are within as well as those who are without, "Let <hi type="italic">your speech be always with grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">v. 6</reference>. Let all your discourse be as becomes Christians, suitable to your profession—savoury, discreet, seasonable." Though it be not always of grace, it must be always with grace; and, though the matter of our discourse be that which is common, yet there must be an air of piety upon it and it must be in a Christian manner <hi type="italic">seasoned with salt.</hi> Grace is the salt which seasons our discourse, makes it savoury, and keeps it from corrupting. <hi type="italic">That you may know how to answer every man.</hi> One answer is proper for one man, and another for another man <reference osisRef="Prov.26.4-Prov.26.5">Prov. xxvi. 4, 5</reference>. We have need of a great deal of wisdom and grace to give proper answers to every man, particularly in answering the questions and objections of adversaries against our religion, giving the reasons of our faith, and showing the unreasonableness of their exceptions and cavils to the best advantage for our cause and least prejudice to ourselves. <hi type="italic">Be ready always to give an answer to every man who asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>.
entries.18d17a69dd465bc6d6defdebd2b69e5013e08895: <div eID="gen32125" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Various Salutations. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen32126" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, <hi type="italic">who is</hi> a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord: <hi type="super">8</hi> Whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that he might know your estate, and comfort your hearts; <hi type="super">9</hi> With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is <hi type="italic">one</hi> of you. They shall make known unto you all things which <hi type="italic">are done</hi> here. <hi type="super">10</hi> Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas, (touching whom ye received commandments: if he come unto you, receive him;) <hi type="super">11</hi> And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only <hi type="italic">are my</hi> fellowworkers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me. <hi type="super">12</hi> Epaphras, who is <hi type="italic">one</hi> of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. <hi type="super">13</hi> For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them <hi type="italic">that are</hi> in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis. <hi type="super">14</hi> Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you. <hi type="super">15</hi> Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house. <hi type="super">16</hi> And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the <hi type="italic">epistle</hi> from Laodicea. <hi type="super">17</hi> And say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfil it. <hi type="super">18</hi> The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you. Amen. <div eID="gen32126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32127" type="x-p"/> In the close of this epistle the apostle does several of his friends the honour to leave their names upon record, with some testimony of his respect, which will be spoken of wherever the gospel comes, and last to the end of the world. <div eID="gen32127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32128" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning Tychicus, <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">v. 7</reference>. By him this epistle was sent; and he does not give them an account in writing of his present state, because Tychicus would do it by word of mouth more fully and particularly. He knew they would be glad to hear how it fared with him. The churches cannot but be concerned for good ministers and desirous to know their state. He gives him this character, <hi type="italic">A beloved brother and faithful minister.</hi> Paul, though a great apostle, owns a faithful minister for a brother and a beloved brother. Faithfulness in any one is truly lovely, and renders him worthy our affection and esteem. <hi type="italic">And a fellow-servant in the Lord.</hi> Ministers are servants to Christ, and fellow-servants to one another. They have one Lord, though they have different stations and capacities of service. Observe, It adds much to the beauty and strength of the gospel ministry when ministers are thus loving and condescending one to another, and by all just means support and advance one another's reputation. Paul sent him not only to tell them of his affairs, but to bring him an account of theirs: <hi type="italic">Whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that he might know your estate, and comfort your hearts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">v. 8</reference>. He was willing to hear from them as they could be to hear from him, and thought himself as much obliged to sympathize with them as he thought them obliged to sympathize with him. It is a great comfort, under the troubles and difficulties of life, to have the mutual concern of fellow-christians. <div eID="gen32128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32129" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning Onesimus (<reference osisRef="Col.4.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.</hi> He was sent back from Rome along with Tychicus. This was he whom Paul had begotten in his bonds, <reference osisRef="Phlm.1.10">Philem. 10</reference>. He had been servant to Philemon, and was a member, if not a minister, of their church. He was converted at Rome, whither he had fled from his master's service; and was now sent back, it is probable, with the epistle to Philemon, to introduce him again into his master's family. Observe, Though he was a poor servant, and had been a bad man, yet, being now a convert, Paul calls him a <hi type="italic">faithful and beloved brother.</hi> The meanest circumstance of life, and greatest wickedness of former life, make no difference in the spiritual relation among sincere Christians: they partake of the same privileges, and are entitles to the same regards. The <hi type="italic">righteousness of God by faith of Jesus Christ is unto all and upon all those that believe; for there is no difference</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.3.22">Rom. iii. 22</reference>): and <hi type="italic">there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither bond nor free, for you are all one in Christ Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.3.28">Gal. iii. 28</reference>. Perhaps this was some time after he was converted and sent back to Philemon, and by this time he had entered into the ministry, because Paul calls him a brother. <div eID="gen32129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32130" type="x-p"/> III. <hi type="italic">Aristarchus, a fellow-prisoner.</hi> Those who join in services and sufferings should be thereby engaged to one another in holy love. Paul had a particular affection for his fellow-servants and his fellow-prisoners. <div eID="gen32130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32131" type="x-p"/> IV. <hi type="italic">Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas.</hi> This is supposed to be the same who wrote the gospel which bears his name. <hi type="italic">If he come unto you receive him.</hi> Paul had a quarrel with Barnabas upon the account of this Mark, who was his nephew, and <hi type="italic">thought not good to take him with them, because he departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.15.38">Acts xv. 38</reference>. He would not take Mark with him, but took Silas, because Mark had deserted them; and yet Paul is not only reconciled to him himself, but recommends him to the respect of the churches, and gives a great example of a truly Christian forgiving spirit. If men have been guilty of a fault, it must not be always remembered against them. We must forget as well as forgive. <hi type="italic">If a man be overtaken in a fault, you who are spiritual restore such a one in the spirit of meekness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.6.1">Gal. vi. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen32131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32132" type="x-p"/> V. Here is one who is called <hi type="italic">Jesus,</hi> which is the Greek name for the Hebrew <hi type="italic">Joshua. If Jesus had given them rest, then would he not afterwards have spoken of another day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.4.8">Heb. iv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who is called Justus.</hi> It is probable that he changed his name for that of Justus, in honour to the name of the Redeemer. Or else Jesus was his Jewish name, for he was of the circumcision; and Justus his Roman or Latin name. <hi type="italic">These are my fellow-labourers unto the kingdom of God, who have been a comfort unto me.</hi> Observe, What comfort the apostle had in the communion of saints and ministers! One is his fellow-servant, another his fellow-prisoner, and all his fellow-workers, who were working out their own salvation and endeavouring to promote the salvation of others. Good ministers take great comfort in those who are their fellow-workers unto the kingdom of God. Their friendship and converse together are a great refreshment under the sufferings and difficulties in their way. <div eID="gen32132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32133" type="x-p"/> VI. <hi type="italic">Epaphras</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.4.12">v. 12</reference>), the same with <hi type="italic">Epaphroditus.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">one of you,</hi> one of your church; <hi type="italic">he salutes you,</hi> or sends his service to you, and his best affections and wishes. <hi type="italic">Always labouring fervently for you in prayers.</hi> Epaphras had learned of Paul to be much in prayer for his friends. Observe, 1. In what manner he prayed for them. He laboured in prayer, laboured fervently, and always laboured fervently for them. Those who would succeed in prayer must take pains in prayer; and we must be earnest in prayer, not only for ourselves, but for others also. It is the effectual fervent prayer which is the prevailing prayer, and availeth much (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jam. v. 16</reference>), and <hi type="italic">Elias prayed earnestly that it might not rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.4.17">v. 17</reference>. 2. What is the matter of this prayer: <hi type="italic">That you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.</hi> Observe, To stand perfect and complete in the will of God is what we should earnestly desire both for ourselves and others. We must stand complete in all the will of God; in the will of his precepts by a universal obedience, and in the will of his providence by a cheerful submission to it: and we stand perfect and complete in both by constancy and perseverance unto the end. The apostle was witness for Epaphras that he had a great zeal for them: "<hi type="italic">I bear him record;</hi> I can testify for him that he has a great concern for you, and that all he does for you proceeds from a warm desire for your good." And his zeal extended to all about them: to <hi type="italic">those who are in Laodicea and Hierapolis.</hi> He had a great concern for the Christian interest in the neighbouring places, as well as among them. <div eID="gen32133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32134" type="x-p"/> VII. <hi type="italic">Luke</hi> is another here mentioned, whom he calls the <hi type="italic">beloved physician.</hi> This is he who wrote the Gospel and Acts, and was Paul's companion. Observe, He was both a physician and an evangelist. Christ himself both taught and healed, and was the great physician as well as prophet of the church. He was the beloved physician; one who recommended himself more than ordinary to the affections of his friends. Skill in physic is a useful accomplishment in a minister and may be improved to more extensive usefulness and greater esteem among Christians. <div eID="gen32134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32135" type="x-p"/> VIII. <hi type="italic">Demas.</hi> Whether this was written before the second epistle to Timothy or after is not certain. There we read (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2 Tim. iv. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world.</hi> Some have thought that this epistle was written after; and then it is an evidence that, though Demas forsook Paul, yet he did not forsake Christ; or he forsook him but for a time, and recovered himself again, and Paul forgave him and owned him as a brother. But others think more probably that this epistle was written before the other; this in <hi type="italic">anno</hi> 62, that in 66, and then it is an evidence how considerable a man Demas was, who yet afterwards revolted. Many who have made a great figure in profession, and gained a great name among Christians, have yet shamefully apostatized: <hi type="italic">They went forth from us, because they were not of us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1 John ii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen32135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32136" type="x-p"/> IX. The <hi type="italic">brethren in Laodicea</hi> are here mentioned, as living in the neighbourhood of Colosse: and Paul sends salutations to them, and orders that this epistle should be read in the church of the Laodiceans (<reference osisRef="Col.4.16">v. 16</reference>), that a copy of it should be sent thither, to be read publicly in their congregation. And some think Paul sent another epistle at this time to Laodicea, and ordered them to send for that from Laodicea, and read it in their church: <hi type="italic">And that you likewise read the epistle from Laodicea.</hi> If so, that epistle is now lost, and did not belong to the canon; for all the epistles which the apostles ever wrote were not preserved, any more than the words and actions of our blessed Lord. <hi type="italic">There are many other things which Jesus did, which if they should be written every one, I suppose the world itself could not contain the books which would be written,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.21.25">John xxi. 25</reference>. But some think it was the epistle to the Ephesians, which is still extant. <div eID="gen32136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32137" type="x-p"/> X. <hi type="italic">Nymphas</hi> is mentioned (<reference osisRef="Col.4.15">v. 15</reference>) as one who lived at Colosse, and had a church in his house; that is, either a religious family, where the several parts of worship were daily performed; or some part of the congregation met there, when they had no public places of worship allowed, and they were forced to assemble in private houses for fear of their enemies. <hi type="italic">The disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.20.19">John xx. 19</reference>), and the apostle preached in his <hi type="italic">own lodging and hired house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.28.23">Acts xxviii. 23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.28.30">30</reference>. In the former sense it showed his exemplary piety; in the latter his zeal and public spirit. <div eID="gen32137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32138" type="x-p"/> XI. Concerning <hi type="italic">Archippus,</hi> who was one of their ministers at Colosse. They are bidden to admonish him to mind his work as a minister, to <hi type="italic">take heed to it, and to fulfil it</hi>—to be diligent and careful of all the parts of it, and to persevere in it unto the end. They must attend to the main design of their ministry, without troubling themselves or the people with things foreign to it, or of less moment. Observe, (1.) The ministry we have received is a great honour; for it is <hi type="italic">received in the Lord,</hi> and is by his appointment and command. (2.) Those who have received it must fulfil it, or do the full duty of it. Those betray their trust, and will have a sad account at last, who <hi type="italic">do this work of the Lord negligently.</hi> (3.) The people may put their ministers in mind of their duty, and excite them to it: <hi type="italic">Say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry,</hi> though no doubt with decency and respect, not from pride and conceit. <div eID="gen32138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32139" type="x-p"/> XII. Concerning himself (<reference osisRef="Col.4.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The salutation of me Paul. Remember my bonds.</hi> He had a scribe to write all the rest of the epistle, but these words he wrote with his own hand: <hi type="italic">Remember my bonds.</hi> He does not say, "Remember I am a prisoner, and send me supply;" but, "Remember I am in bonds as the apostle of the Gentiles, and let this confirm your faith in the gospel of Christ:" it adds weight to this exhortation: <hi type="italic">I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you to walk worthy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.1">Eph. iv. 1</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Grace be with you.</hi> The favour of God, and all good, the blessed fruits and effects of it, be with you, and be your portion."  <chapter eID="Col.4"/> <div eID="gen32139" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32026" osisID="Col" type="book"/>

Alford translates, "fairness," "equity," which gives a large and liberal interpretation of justice in common matters (Phm 16).<div eID="gen36517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knowing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.3.24">Col 3:24</reference>).<div eID="gen36518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye also--</hi>as well as they. <div eID="gen36519" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cb2afd9b90d0ecd73cad539949b1725df1943fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17903"/><div sID="gen36520" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17903"/><hi type="bold">2. Continue--</hi>Greek, "Continue perseveringly," "persevere" (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.18">Ep 6:18</reference>), "watching thereunto"; here, "watch in the same," or "in it," that is, in prayer: watching against the indolence as to prayer, and in prayer, of our corrupt wills.<div eID="gen36520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with thanksgiving--</hi>for everything, whether joyful, or sorrowful, mercies temporal and spiritual, national, family, and individual (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.17">1Co 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.6">Php 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.18">1Th 5:18</reference>). <div eID="gen36521" type="x-p"/>
entries.61588d7a6d2917e61bf8e0739c39eb6fce2de56a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17904"/><div sID="gen36522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17904"/><hi type="bold">3. for us--</hi>myself and Timothy (<reference osisRef="Col.1.1">Col 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a door of utterance--</hi>Translate, "a door for the word." Not as in <reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>, where power of "utterance" is his petition. Here it is an opportunity for preaching the word, which would be best afforded by his release from prison (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">1Co 16:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Co 2:12</reference>; Phm 22; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.8">Re 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36524" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to speak--</hi>so that we may speak.<div eID="gen36524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36525" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the mystery of Christ--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Col.1.27">Col 1:27</reference>).<div eID="gen36525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36526" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for which ... also--</hi>on account of which I am (not only "an ambassador," <reference osisRef="Eph.6.20">Ep 6:20</reference>, but) ALSO in bonds. <div eID="gen36526" type="x-p"/>
entries.266647f6074122f9860bede2aa2f6e38af156478: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17905"/><div sID="gen36527" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17905"/>4. Alford thinks that Paul asks their prayers for his release as if it were the "only" way by which he could "make it (the Gospel) manifest" as he ought. But while this is included in their subject of prayer, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Php 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.13">13</reference>, written somewhat later in his imprisonment, clearly shows that "a door for the word" could be opened, and was opened, for its manifestation, even while he remained imprisoned (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.9">2Ti 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen36527" type="x-p"/>
entries.b64821a2698f242eae2139ddfc80c093d6de680c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17906"/><div sID="gen36528" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17906"/>5. (See on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">Ep 5:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">16</reference>.)<div eID="gen36528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36529" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in wisdom--</hi>practical Christian prudence.<div eID="gen36529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them ... without--</hi>Those not in the Christian brotherhood (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.12">1Co 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.4.12">1Th 4:12</reference>). The brethren, through love, will make allowances for an indiscreet act or word of a brother; the world will make none. Therefore be the more on your guard in your intercourse with the latter, lest you be a stumbling-block to their conversion.<div eID="gen36530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeeming the time--</hi>The Greek expresses, buying up for yourselves, and buying off from worldly vanities the opportunity, whenever it is afforded you, of good to yourselves and others. "Forestall the opportunity, that is, to buy up an article out of the market, so as to make the largest profit from it" [Conybeare and Howson]. <div eID="gen36531" type="x-p"/>
entries.825b99a7b62602cf7d6f61cbfe69586e4719cfea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17907"/><div sID="gen36532" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17907"/><hi type="bold">6. with grace--</hi>Greek, "IN grace" as its element (<reference osisRef="Col.3.16">Col 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.29">Ep 4:29</reference>). Contrast the case of those "of the world" who "therefore speak of the world" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.5">1Jo 4:5</reference>). Even the smallest leaf of the believer should be full of the sap of the Holy Spirit (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.7">Jr 17:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">8</reference>). His conversation should be cheerful without levity, serious without gloom. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Lu 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.46">Joh 7:46</reference>, as to Jesus' speech.<div eID="gen36532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seasoned with salt--</hi>that is, the savor of fresh and lively spiritual wisdom and earnestness, excluding all "corrupt communication," and also tasteless insipidity (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.13">Mt 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.50">Mr 9:50</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.29">Ep 4:29</reference>). Compare all the sacrifices seasoned with salt (<reference osisRef="Lev.2.13">Le 2:13</reference>). Not far from Colosse, in Phrygia, there was a salt lake, which gives to the image here the more appropriateness.<div eID="gen36533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36534" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how ye ought to answer every man--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1Pe 3:15</reference>). <div eID="gen36534" type="x-p"/>
entries.81c3956cf2fb874728c8d2cee77928c1a723ab2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17908"/><div sID="gen36535" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17908"/><hi type="bold">7. Tychicus--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">Ep 6:2</reference>).<div eID="gen36535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36536" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who is a beloved brother--</hi>rather, "the beloved brother"; the article "the" marks him as well known to them. <div eID="gen36536" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9df74a95a0cbc25a510b3ec00306bcc1007dcf8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17909"/><div sID="gen36537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17909"/><hi type="bold">8. for the same purpose--</hi>Greek, "for this very purpose."<div eID="gen36537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36538" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he might know your estate--</hi>Translate, "that he may know your state": answering to <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>. So one very old manuscript and Vulgate read. But the oldest manuscripts and the old Latin versions, "that YE may know OUR state." However, the latter reading seems likely to have crept in from <reference osisRef="Eph.6.22">Ep 6:22</reference>. Paul was the more anxious to know the state of the Colossians, on account of the seductions to which they were exposed from false teachers; owing to which he had "great conflict for" them (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>).<div eID="gen36538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36539" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">comfort your hearts--</hi>distressed as ye are by my imprisonment, as well as by your own trials. <div eID="gen36539" type="x-p"/>
entries.b33bf4b7fe5fe2b12cce8c2d728f1a16fe93758b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17910"/><div sID="gen36540" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17910"/><hi type="bold">9. Onesimus--</hi>the slave mentioned in the Epistle to Philemon (Phm 10, 16), "a brother beloved."<div eID="gen36540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a faithful ... brother--</hi>rather, "the faithful brother," he being known to the Colossians as the slave of Philemon, their fellow townsman and fellow Christian.<div eID="gen36541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one of you--</hi>belonging to your city.<div eID="gen36542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They shall make known unto you all things--</hi>Greek, "all the things here." This substantial repetition of "all my state shall Tychicus declare unto you," strongly favors the reading of English Version in <reference osisRef="Col.4.8">Col 4:8</reference>, "that he might (may) know your state," as it is unlikely the same thing should be stated thrice. <div eID="gen36543" type="x-p"/>
entries.c94dd942e99ac10707845e28cc7d5fb4f76136b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17911"/><div sID="gen36544" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17911"/><hi type="bold">10. Aristarchus--</hi>a Macedonian of Thessalonica (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.2">Ac 27:2</reference>), who was dragged into the theater at Ephesus, during the tumult with Gaius, they being "Paul's companions in travel." He accompanied Paul to Asia (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.4">Ac 20:4</reference>), and subsequently (<reference osisRef="Acts.27.2">Ac 27:2</reference>) to Rome. He was now at Rome with Paul (compare Phm 23, 24). As he is here spoken of as Paul's "fellow prisoner," but in Phm 24 as Paul's "fellow laborer"; and vice versa, Epaphras in Phm 23, as his "fellow prisoner," but here (<reference osisRef="Col.1.7">Col 1:7</reference>) "fellow servant," Meyer in Alford, conjectures that Paul's friends voluntarily shared his imprisonment by turns, Aristarchus being his fellow prisoner when he wrote to the Colossians, Epaphras when he wrote to Philemon. The Greek for "fellow prisoner" is literally, fellow captive, an image from prisoners taken in warfare, Christians being "fellow soldiers" (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.25">Php 2:25</reference>; Phm 2), whose warfare is "the good fight of faith."<div eID="gen36544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36545" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Mark--</hi>John Mark (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Ac 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.25">25</reference>); the Evangelist according to tradition.<div eID="gen36545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sister's son--</hi>rather, "cousin," or "kinsman to Barnabas"; the latter being the better known is introduced to designate Mark. The relationship naturally accounts for Barnabas' selection of Mark as his companion when otherwise qualified; and also for Mark's mother's house at Jerusalem being the place of resort of Christians there (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.12">Ac 12:12</reference>). The family belonged to Cyprus (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.36">Ac 4:36</reference>); this accounts for Barnabas' choice of Cyprus as the first station on their journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.4">Ac 13:4</reference>), and for Mark's accompanying them readily so far, it being the country of his family; and for Paul's rejecting him at the second journey for not having gone further than Perga, in Pamphylia, but having gone thence home to his mother at Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.37">Mt 10:37</reference>) on the first journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.13">Ac 13:13</reference>).<div eID="gen36546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36547" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">touching whom--</hi>namely, Mark.<div eID="gen36547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36548" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye received commandments--</hi>possibly before the writing of this Epistle; or the "commandments" were verbal by Tychicus, and accompanying this letter, since the past tense was used by the ancients (where we use the present) in relation to the time which it would be when the letter was read by the Colossians. Thus (Phm 19), "I have written," for "I write." The substance of them was, "If he come unto you, receive him." Paul's rejection of him on his second missionary journey, because he had turned back at Perga on the first journey (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.13">Ac 13:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.37-Acts.15.39">15:37-39</reference>), had caused an alienation between himself and Barnabas. Christian love soon healed the breach; for here he implies his restored confidence in Mark, makes honorable allusion to Barnabas, and desires that those at Colosse who had regarded Mark in consequence of that past error with suspicion, should now "receive" him with kindness. Colosse is only about one hundred ten miles from Perga, and less than twenty from the confines of Pisidia, through which province Paul and Barnabas preached on their return during the same journey. Hence, though Paul had not personally visited the Colossian Church, they knew of the past unfaithfulness of Mark; and needed this recommendation of him, after the temporary cloud on him, so as to receive him, now that he was about to visit them as an evangelist. Again, in Paul's last imprisonment, he, for the last time, speaks of Mark (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen36548" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a4320c066b7b39da3b84a9068d46fa2927d7ab1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17912"/><div sID="gen36549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17912"/><hi type="bold">11. Justus--</hi>that is, righteous; a common name among the Jews; Hebrew, "tzadik" (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.23">Ac 1:23</reference>).<div eID="gen36549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the circumcision--</hi>This implies that Epaphras, Luke, and Demas (<reference osisRef="Col.4.12">Col 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.14">14</reference>) were not of the circumcision. This agrees with Luke's Gentile name (the same as Lucanus), and the Gentile aspect of his Gospel.<div eID="gen36550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">These only, &c.--</hi>namely, of the Jews. For the Jewish teachers were generally opposed to the apostle of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.15">Php 1:15</reference>). Epaphras, &c., were also fellow laborers, but Gentiles.<div eID="gen36551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto--</hi>that is, in promoting the Gospel kingdom.<div eID="gen36552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36553" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which have been--</hi>Greek, "which have been made," or "have become," that is, inasmuch as they have become a comfort to me. The Greek implies comfort in forensic dangers; a different Greek word expresses comfort in domestic affliction [Bengel]. <div eID="gen36553" type="x-p"/>
entries.586153c4a855390415ee0b80026006b0626b8367: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17913"/><div sID="gen36554" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17913"/><hi type="bold">12. Christ--</hi>The oldest manuscripts add "Jesus."<div eID="gen36554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36555" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labouring fervently--</hi>As the Greek, is the same, translate, "striving earnestly" (see on <reference osisRef="Col.1.29">Col 1:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>), literally, "striving as in the agony of a contest."<div eID="gen36555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in prayers--</hi>Translate as Greek, "in his prayers."<div eID="gen36556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36557" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">complete--</hi>The oldest manuscripts read, "fully assured." It is translated, "fully persuaded," <reference osisRef="Rom.4.21">Ro 4:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.5">14:5</reference>. In the expression "perfect," he refers to what he has already said, <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col 1:28</reference>; 2:<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2; 3:14</reference>. "Perfect" implies the attainment of the full maturity of a Christian. Bengel joins "in all the will of God" with "stand." <div eID="gen36557" type="x-p"/>
entries.30ba3a48e639e15f2f46121c3a0fa40a926fea12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17914"/><div sID="gen36558" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17914"/><hi type="bold">13. a great zeal--</hi>The oldest manuscripts and Vulgate have "much labor."<div eID="gen36558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36559" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for you--</hi>lest you should be seduced (<reference osisRef="Col.2.4">Col 2:4</reference>); a motive why you should be anxious for yourselves.<div eID="gen36559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36560" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them that are in Laodicea ... Hierapolis--</hi>churches probably founded by Epaphras, as the Church in Colosse was. Laodicea, called from Laodice, queen of Antiochus II, on the river Lycus, was, according to the subscription to First Timothy, "the chiefest city of Phrygia Pacatiana" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.21">1Ti 6:21</reference>). All the three cities were destroyed by an earthquake in A.D. 62 [Tacitus, Annals, 14.27]. Hierapolis was six Roman miles north of Laodicea. <div eID="gen36560" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7487e91d266c49620b0650273e6a40f9441cabf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17915"/><div sID="gen36561" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17915"/>14. It is conjectured that Luke "the beloved physician" (the same as the Evangelist), may have first become connected with Paul in professionally attending on him in the sickness under which he labored in Phrygia and Galatia (in which latter place he was detained by sickness), in the early part of that journey wherein Luke first is found in his company (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.10">Ac 16:10</reference>; compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>). Thus the allusion to his medical profession is appropriate in writing to men of Phrygia. Luke ministered to Paul in his last imprisonment (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Ti 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen36561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36562" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Demas--</hi>included among his "fellow laborers" (Phm 24), but afterwards a deserter from him through love of this world (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.10">2Ti 4:10</reference>). He alone has here no honorable or descriptive epithet attached to his name. Perhaps, already, his real character was betraying itself. <div eID="gen36562" type="x-p"/>
entries.f745fef7106ea042fa72012a16ad8dbeb20b9a15: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17916"/><div sID="gen36563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17916"/><hi type="bold">15. Nymphas--</hi>of Laodicea.<div eID="gen36563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">church ... in his house--</hi>So old manuscripts and Vulgate read. The oldest read, "THEIR house"; and one manuscript, "HER house," which makes Nymphas a woman. <div eID="gen36564" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac3e892bb313d8258ff955de76347a61ddc1ffa2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17917"/><div sID="gen36565" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17917"/><hi type="bold">16. the epistle from Laodicea--</hi>namely, the Epistle which I wrote to the Laodiceans, and which you will get from them on applying to them. Not the Epistle to the Ephesians. See Introduction to Ephesians and Introduction to Colossians. The Epistles from the apostles were publicly read in the church assemblies. Ignatius [Epistle to the Ephesians, 12], Polycarp [Epistle to the Philippians, 3.11,12], Clement [Epistle to the Corinthians, 1. 47], <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.27">1Th 5:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.3">Re 1:3</reference>, "Blessed is he that readeth, and they that hear." Thus, they and the Gospels were put on a level with the Old Testament, which was similarly read (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.11">De 31:11</reference>). The Holy Spirit inspired Paul to write, besides those extant, other Epistles which He saw necessary for that day, and for particular churches; and which were not so for the Church of all ages and places. It is possible that as the Epistle to the Colossians was to be read for the edification of other churches besides that of Colosse; so the Epistle to the Ephesians was to be read in various churches besides Ephesus, and that Laodicea was the last of such churches before Colosse, whence he might designate the Epistle to the Ephesians here as "the Epistle from Laodicea." But it is equally possible that the Epistle meant was one to the Laodiceans themselves. <div eID="gen36565" type="x-p"/>
entries.fcd6fc4b2e35d2cb4901a5210823333160233509: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17918"/><div sID="gen36566" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17918"/><hi type="bold">17. say to Archippus--</hi>The Colossians (not merely the clergy, but the laymen) are directed, "Speak ye to Archippus." This proves that Scripture belongs to the laity as well as the clergy; and that laymen may profitably admonish the clergy in particular cases when they do so in meekness. Bengel suggests that Archippus was perhaps prevented from going to the Church assembly by weak health or age. The word, "fulfil," accords with his ministry being near its close (<reference osisRef="Col.1.25">Col 1:25</reference>; compare Phm 2). However, "fulfil" may mean, as in <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.5">2Ti 4:5</reference>, "make full proof of thy ministry." "Give all diligence to follow it out fully"; a monition perhaps needed by Archippus.<div eID="gen36566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the Lord--</hi>The element in which every work of the Christian, and especially the Christian minister, is to be done (<reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.39">1Co 7:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.2">Php 4:2</reference>). <div eID="gen36567" type="x-p"/>
entries.8545c9624330f20e04d6500d7a5c94bd853bf6a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17919"/><div sID="gen36568" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17919"/>18. Paul's autograph salutation (so <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.21">1Co 16:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.17">2Th 3:17</reference>), attesting that the preceding letter, though written by an amanuensis, is from himself.<div eID="gen36568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36569" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Remember my bonds--</hi>Already in this chapter he had mentioned his "bonds" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.3">Col 4:3</reference>), and again <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, an incentive why they should love and pray (<reference osisRef="Col.4.3">Col 4:3</reference>) for him; and still more, that they should, in reverential obedience to his monitions in this Epistle, shrink from the false teaching herein stigmatized, remembering what a conflict (<reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>) he had in their behalf amidst his bonds. "When we read of his chains, we should not forget that they moved over the paper as he wrote; his [right] hand was chained to the [left hand of the] soldier who kept him" [Alford].<div eID="gen36569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36570" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Grace be with you--</hi>Greek, "THE grace" which every Christian enjoys in some degree, and which flows from God in Christ by the Holy Ghost (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.15">Tit 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.25">He 13:25</reference>) <chapter eID="Col.4"/><div eID="gen36570" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen36198" osisID="Col" type="book"/>

entries.4e6f9f2c9461324add64926d90cf55cfb8d47666: <div eID="gen50980" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen50981" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50982" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50982" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen50981" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen50983" type="x-p"/> The duty of masters to their servants, <reference osisRef="Col.4.1">Col 4:1</reference>. Continuance in prayer recommended, to which watchfulness and thanksgiving should be joined, <reference osisRef="Col.4.2">Col 4:2</reference>. And to pray particularly for the success of the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Col.4.3">Col 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.4">Col 4:4</reference>. Directions concerning walking wisely, redeeming of time, and godly conversation, <reference osisRef="Col.4.5">Col 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.4.6">Col 4:6</reference>. He refers them to Tychicus and Onesimus, whom he sends to them for particulars relative to his present circumstances, <reference osisRef="Col.4.7-Col.4.9">Col 4:7-9</reference>. Mentions the salutations of several then at Rome, of whom he gives some interesting particulars, <reference osisRef="Col.4.10-Col.4.14">Col 4:10-14</reference>. Sends his own salutations to the brethren in Laodicea, and to Nymphas and the Church at his house, <reference osisRef="Col.4.15">Col 4:15</reference>. Directs this epistle to be read in the Church of the Laodiceans, and that to them to be read at Colosse, <reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>. Directions to Archippus relative to his ministry, <reference osisRef="Col.4.17">Col 4:17</reference>. Concludes with salutations to the people at Colosse, to whom he sends his apostolical benediction, <reference osisRef="Col.4.18">Col 4:18</reference>. <div eID="gen50983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50984" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen50984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50985" type="x-p"/> Masters, give unto your servants - This verse should have been added to the preceding, to which it properly belongs; and this chapter should have begun with <reference osisRef="Col.4.2">Col 4:2</reference>. <div eID="gen50985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50986" type="x-p"/> That which is just and equal - As they are bondmen or slaves of whom the apostle speaks, we may at once see with what propriety this exhortation is given. The condition of slaves among the Greeks and Romans was wretched in the extreme; they could appeal to no law; and they could neither expect justice nor equity. The apostle, therefore, informs the proprietors of these slaves that they should act towards them both according to justice and equity; for God, their Master, required this of them, and would at last call them to account for their conduct in this respect. Justice and equity required that they should have proper food, proper raiment, due rest, and no more than moderate work. This is a lesson that all masters throughout the universe should carefully learn. Do not treat your servants as if God had made them of an inferior blood to yours.
entries.911aa8aa4c22d8b67bcbe046a6ad2199dccc47d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen50986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50987" type="x-p"/> Continue in prayer - This was the apostle's general advice to all; without this, neither wives, husbands, children, parents, servants, nor masters, could fulfill the duties which God, in their respective stations, required of them. <div eID="gen50987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50988" type="x-p"/> All might, power, and life come from God; his creatures are continually dependent upon him for all these: to earnest, persevering prayer, he has promised every supply; but he who prays not has no promise. How few wives feel it their duty to pray to God to give them grace to behave as wives! How few husbands pray for the grace suited to their situation, that they may be able to fulfill its duties! The like may be said of children, parents, servants, and masters. As every situation in life has its peculiar duties, trials, etc.; so to every situation there is peculiar grace appointed. No man can fulfill the duties of any station without the grace suited to that station. The grace suited to him, as a member of society in general, will not be sufficient for him as a husband, father, or master. Many proper marriages become unhappy in the end, because the parties have not earnestly besought God for the grace necessary for them as husbands and wives. This is the origin of family broils in general; and a proper attention to the apostle's advice would prevent them all. <div eID="gen50988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50989" type="x-p"/> Watch in the same - Be always on your guard; and when you have got the requisite grace by praying, take care of it, and bring it into its proper action by watchfulness; by which you will know when, and where, and how to apply it. <div eID="gen50989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50990" type="x-p"/> With thanksgiving - Being always grateful to God, who has called you into such a state of salvation, and affords you such abundant means and opportunities to glorify him.
entries.ef4554dce3bca0d9aeb5e28519764beb14ef0419: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen50990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50991" type="x-p"/> Praying also for us - Let the success and spread of the Gospel be ever dear to you; and neglect not to pray fervently to God that it may have free course, run, and be glorified. <div eID="gen50991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50992" type="x-p"/> A door of utterance - Θυραν του λογου· The word θυρα, which commonly signifies a door, or such like entrance into a house or passage through a wall, is often used metaphorically for an entrance to any business, occasion or opportunity to commence or perform any particular work. So in <reference osisRef="Act.14.27">Act 14:27</reference> : The Door of faith is opened to the Gentiles; i.e. there is now an opportunity of preaching the Gospel to the nations of the earth. <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.9">1Cor 16:9</reference> : A great and effectual Door is opened unto me; i.e. I have now a glorious opportunity of preaching the truth to the people of Ephesus. <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">2Cor 2:12</reference> : When I came to Troas - a Door was opened unto me; I had a fine opportunity of preaching Christ crucified at that place. So, here, the θυρατου λογου, which we translate door of utterance, signifies an occasion, opportunity, or entrance, for the doctrine of the Gospel. The same metaphor is used by the best Latin writers. Cicero, xiii. Ep. 10: Amiciliae fores aperiuntur; the Doors of friendship are opened - there is now an opportunity of reconciliation. And Ovid, Amor. lib. iii., Eleg. xii. ver. 12: - <div eID="gen50992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50993" type="x-p"/> Janua per nostras est adaperta manus. "The gate is opened by our hands." <div eID="gen50993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50994" type="x-p"/> Of this use of the word among the Greek writers Schleusner gives several examples. See also <reference osisRef="Rev.3.8">Rev 3:8</reference>, where the word is used in the same sense. To multiply examples would be needless; the apostle excites them to pray, not that a door of utterance, i.e. a readiness and fluency of speech, may be given to him and his fellow laborers, but that they may have an opportunity of preaching the doctrine of Christ; and so the term λογος is to be understood here, as well as in many other places of the New Testament, in most of which we have either lost or obscured its meaning by translating it word instead of doctrine. <div eID="gen50994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50995" type="x-p"/> The mystery of Christ - The Gospel, which had been hidden from all former times, and which revealed that purpose long hidden in the Divine councils, that the Gentiles should be called to enjoy the same privileges with the Jews. <div eID="gen50995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50996" type="x-p"/> For which I am also in bonds - He was suffering under Jewish malice, and for preaching this very mystery; for they could not bear to hear announced, as from heaven, that the Gentiles, whom they considered eternally shut out from any participation of the Divine favor, should be made fellow heirs with them of the grace of life; much less could they bear to hear that they were about to be reprobated, and the Gentiles elected in their place. It was for asserting these things that they persecuted Paul at Jerusalem, so that to save his life he was obliged to appeal to Caesar; and being taken to Rome, he was detained a prisoner till his case was fully heard; and he was a prisoner at Rome on this very account when he wrote this Epistle to the Colossians. See the note on <reference osisRef="Col.1.24">Col 1:24</reference>.
entries.987812268279953cca54e668b6a387b166606181: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen50996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50997" type="x-p"/> That I may make it manifest - It was a mystery, and he wished to make it manifest - to lay it open, and make all men see it.
entries.b4a9ef0e34d7b5f5fbf75eb941fa03800afd0577: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen50997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50998" type="x-p"/> Walk in wisdom - Act wisely and prudently in reference to them who are without - who yet continue unbelieving Gentiles or persecuting Jews. <div eID="gen50998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen50999" type="x-p"/> The Church of Christ was considered an enclosure; a field, or vineyard, well hedged or walled. Those who were not members of it, were considered without; i.e. not under that especial protection and defense which the true followers of Christ had. This has been since called "The pale of the Church," from palus, a stake; or, as Dr. Johnson defines it, "A narrow piece of wood, joined above and below to a rail, to enclose grounds." As to be a Christian was essential to the salvation of the soul, so to be in the Church of Christ was essential to the being a Christian; therefore it was concluded that "there was no salvation out of the pale of the Church." Now this is true in all places where the doctrines of Christianity are preached; but when one description of people professing Christianity, with their own peculiar mode of worship and creed, arrogate to themselves, exclusive of all others, the title of The Church; and then, on the ground of a maxim which is true in itself, but falsely understood and applied by them, assert that, as they are The Church, and there is no Church besides, then you must be one of them, believe as they believe, and worship as they worship, or you will be infallibly damned; I say, when this is asserted, every man who feels he has an immortal spirit is called on to examine the pretensions of such spiritual monopolists. Now, as the Church of Christ is formed on the foundation of the prophets and apostles, Jesus Christ being the chief corner stone, the doctrines of this Christian Church must be sought for in the sacred Scriptures. As to fathers, councils, and human authorities of all kinds, they are, in this question, lighter than vanity; the book of God alone must decide. The Church, which has been so hasty to condemn all others, and, by its own soi disant or self-constituted authority, to make itself the determiner of the fates of men, dealing out the mansions of glory to its partisans, and the abodes of endless misery to all those who are out of its antichristian and inhuman pale; this Church, I say, has been brought to this standard, and proved by the Scriptures to be fallen from the faith of God's elect, and to be most awfully and dangerously corrupt; and to be within its pale, of all others professing Christianity, would be the most likely means of endangering the final salvation of the soul. Yet even in it many sincere and upright persons may be found, who, in spirit and practice, belong to the true Church of Christ. Such persons are to be found of all religious persuasions, and in all sorts of Christian societies. <div eID="gen50999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51000" type="x-p"/> Redeeming the time - See on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.16">Eph 5:16</reference> (note).
entries.b9455fbd5f31efe07c9a192aacb854160e4ae449: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51001" type="x-p"/> Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt - Let it be such as has a tendency to oppose and preserve from the corruption of sin. The rabbins say: "He who, in prayer, omits any word, should begin again at the beginning; for he who does not is like boiled pottage, in which there is no salt." Berachoth, fol. 34, 1. Let all your conversation be such as may tend to exemplify and recommend Christianity; let it not only be holy, but wise, gracious, and intelligent. A harsh method of proposing or defending the doctrines of Christianity only serves to repel men from those doctrines, and from the way of salvation. Salt, from its use in preserving food from corruption, and rendering it both savoury and wholesome, has always been made the emblem of wisdom. The word has been also used to express in composition or conversation what is terse, comprehensive, useful, elegant, and impressive. The term Attic salt has been used to express some of the principal beauties of the Greek tongue; of such beauties the Gospel of Christ has an endless store. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.5.13">Mat 5:13</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Mar.9.50">Mar 9:50</reference> (note). <div eID="gen51001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51002" type="x-p"/> How ye ought to answer every man - That your discourse may be so judiciously managed, that ye may discern how to treat the prejudices and meet the objections both of Jews and Gentiles.
entries.ed14cdc5ab5a4ea939e10ef0d8bdb671fa8e3f67: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51003" type="x-p"/> All my state shall Tychicus - See the note on <reference osisRef="Eph.6.21">Eph 6:21</reference>. Tychicus well knew the apostle's zeal and perseverance in preaching the Gospel, his sufferings on that account, his success in converting both Jews and Gentiles, and the converts which were made in Caesar's household; he could give these to the Colossians in ample detail, and some of them it would not have been prudent to commit to writing.
entries.7aec7a6fdc87b1d73114af9158cbcdfc3cb566e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51004" type="x-p"/> That he might know your estate - Instead of ἱνα γνῳ τα περι ὑμων, that He may know Your affairs, ABD*FG, many others, with the Ethiopic, Itala, Theodoret, and Damascenus, read ἱνα γνωτε τα περι ἡμων, that Ye may know Our affairs; which is probably the true reading. Tychicus was sent to them, not to know their affairs, but with Onesimus, to carry this epistle and make the apostle's state known to them, and comfort their hearts by the good news which he brought. The next verse confirms this meaning.
entries.56627ca2b7dc9508def71ba2d0e515b74b697c25: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51005" type="x-p"/> With Onesimus - who is one of you - Onesimus was a native of some part of Phrygia, if not of Colosse itself; and being lately converted to the Christian faith by the instrumentality of the apostle, he would be able, on this account, to give them satisfactory information concerning the apostle's state, which would be doubly acceptable to them as he was their countryman. See the Epistle to Philemon. <div eID="gen51005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51006" type="x-p"/> All things which are done here - FG, the Vulgate, Itala, Jerome, and Bede, add here πραττομενα, what is done, which we have supplied in Italics in our translation. These brethren could give an account of the transactions at Rome, relative to the apostle and Christianity, which it might not be prudent for him to commit to writing. See on <reference osisRef="Col.4.7">Col 4:7</reference> (note). The reign of Nero was not only cruel, but suspicious, jealous, and dangerous.
entries.1aba016f89f3a38193e0c07554c74ac55e1dad16: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51007" type="x-p"/> Aristarchus my fellow prisoner - Concerning Aristarchus, see <reference osisRef="Act.19.29">Act 19:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.20.4">Act 20:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.27.2">Act 27:2</reference>; and see the note on <reference osisRef="Act.27.2">Act 27:2</reference>. Aristarchus and Epaphras are mentioned as saluters in this epistle, and in that to Philemon written at the same time; but here he is said to be a prisoner, and Epaphras not. In that to Philemon, Epaphras is called a prisoner, and Aristarchus not. One of them is wrong, though it is uncertain which; unless both were prisoners. See Wall's Crit. Notes. As Aristarchus had been a zealous and affectionate adherent to St. Paul, and followed him in all his journeys, ministering to him in prison, and assisting him in preaching the Gospel in Rome, he might have been imprisoned on this account. We need not suppose that both he and Epaphras were imprisoned at the same time; about the same time they might be imprisoned, but it might be so ordered by the providence of God that when Aristarchus was imprisoned Epaphras was at liberty, and while Epaphras was in prison Aristarchus was at liberty. This is a very possible and easily to be conceived case. <div eID="gen51007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51008" type="x-p"/> Marcus - See the account of this person, <reference osisRef="Act.15.39">Act 15:39</reference>. Though there had been some difference between the apostle and this Mark, yet from this, and <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Tim 4:11</reference>, we find that they were fully reconciled, and that Mark was very useful to St. Paul in the work of the ministry. <div eID="gen51008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51009" type="x-p"/> Touching whom ye received commandments - What these were we cannot tell; it was some private communication which had been previously sent to the Colossian Church.
entries.66233d81c9ba3c55e4cedc0f5c07f17b5679bce3: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen51009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51010" type="x-p"/> Jesus, which is called Justus - Jesus, Joshua, or Jehoshua, was his name among his countrymen the Jews; Justus was the name which he bore among the Greeks and Romans. <div eID="gen51010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51011" type="x-p"/> These only - That is, only Aristarchus, Marcus, and Jesus Justus, who were formerly Jews or proselytes; for οἱ οντες εκ περιτομης, they were of the circumcision, and assisted the apostle in preaching the Gospel. There were others who did preach Christianity, but they did it from envy and strife, in order to add affliction to the apostle's bonds. It is evident, therefore, that St. Peter was not now at Rome, else he certainly would have been mentioned in this list; for we cannot suppose that he was in the list of those who preached Christ in an exceptionable way, and from impure and unholy motives: indeed, there is no evidence that St. Peter ever saw Rome. And as it cannot be proved that he ever was bishop or pope of that city, the keystone of the triumphal arch of the pope of Rome is pulled out; this building, therefore, of his supremacy, cannot stand.
entries.bcf3585650cf45a11dbeaf2d99b6b32e0fe842db: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen51011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51012" type="x-p"/> Epaphras, who is one of you - A native of some part of Phrygia, and probably of Colosse itself. <div eID="gen51012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51013" type="x-p"/> A servant of Christ - A minister of the Gospel. <div eID="gen51013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51014" type="x-p"/> Labouring fervently for you - Αγωνιζομενος· Agonizing; very properly expressed by our translators, labouring fervently. <div eID="gen51014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51015" type="x-p"/> That ye may stand perfect and complete - Ἱνα στητε τελειοι και πεπληρμενοι. That ye may stand firm, perfectly instructed, and fully persuaded of the truth of those doctrines which have been taught you as the revealed will of God: this I believe to be the meaning of the apostle. <div eID="gen51015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51016" type="x-p"/> Instead of πεπληρωμενοι, complete or filled up, almost all the MSS. of the Alexandrian rescension, which are considered the most authentic and correct, have πεπληροφορημενοι, that ye may be fully persuaded. The word πληροφορια signifies such a complete persuasion of the certainty of a thing, as leaves the mind which has it neither room nor inclination to doubt; and πληροφορεω, the verb, has the same meaning, viz., to be thus persuaded, or to persuade thus, by demonstrative argumentation and exhibition of unquestionable facts. <div eID="gen51016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51017" type="x-p"/> This is such a persuasion as the Spirit of God, by means of the Gospel, gives to every sincere and faithful man; and from which arises the solid happiness of the genuine Christian. They who argue against it, prove, at least, that they have not got it.
entries.26644a2b1febdbc99ec00a0a81ccf1df831d2e18: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen51017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51018" type="x-p"/> He hath a great zeal for you - Instead of ζηλον πολυν, much zeal, ABCD**, several others, with versions and fathers, read πολυν πονον, much labor; they are here nearly of the same meaning, though the latter appears to be the better and genuine reading. <div eID="gen51018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51019" type="x-p"/> Laodicea, and - Hierapolis - These were both cities of Phrygia, between which Colosse, or the city of Colassa, was situated. See <reference osisRef="Col.2.1">Col 2:1</reference>. The latter was called Hierapolis, or the holy city, from the multitude of its temples. Apollo, Diana, Esculapius, and Hygeia, were all worshipped here, as appears by the coins of this city still extant.
entries.561ad84fe183ecd0330426ee33db0483c4fead4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen51019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51020" type="x-p"/> Luke, the beloved physician - This is generally supposed to be the same with Luke the evangelist. See the preface to the notes on this gospel. Some, however, suppose them to be different persons; because, where it is evident that Luke the evangelist is meant, he never has more than his simple name Luke; and because the apostle is supposed to intend a different person here, he adds, ὁ ιατρος ὁ αγαπητος, the beloved physician. The word ιατρος signifies a healer, and must not be restricted to physician, in the sense in which we use that word; he was surgeon, physician, and dispenser of medicines, etc., for all these were frequently combined in the same person.
entries.b39dc3240bf2ccb52366433b30a2ca2b0df62d6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen51020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51021" type="x-p"/> Salute - Nymphas, and the Church - in his house - This person, and his whole family, which probably was very numerous, appear to have received the Gospel; and it seems that, for their benefit and that of his neighbors, he had opened his house for the worship of God. In those primitive times there were no consecrated places, for it was supposed that the simple setting apart of any place for the worship of God was a sufficient consecration. See of those domestic churches, <reference osisRef="Rom.16.5">Rom 16:5</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.19">1Cor 16:19</reference> (note)
entries.330421eab8a8851745da873c9a339a4247a5fb30: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen51021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51022" type="x-p"/> Cause that it be read also in the Church of the Laodiceans - That is: Let a copy be taken, and sent to them, that it may be read there also. This appears to have been a regular custom in the apostolic Church. <div eID="gen51022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51023" type="x-p"/> That ye likewise read the epistle from Laodicea - Some suppose that this was an epistle sent from Laodicea to the apostle, which he now sent by Aristarchus to the Colossians, that they might peruse it; that thereby they might see the propriety of sending a copy of his epistle to them, to the Laodicean Church. Many eminent critics are of this opinion, which appears to me to be both forced and far fetched. Others think that the Epistle to the Ephesians is the epistle in question, and that it was originally directed to them, and not to the Ephesians. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Eph.1.1">Eph 1:1</reference>, etc. But others, equally learned, think that there was an epistle, different from that to the Ephesians, sent by St. Paul to the Laodiceans, which is now lost. There was an epistle under this direction in the times of Theodoret and Jerome, for both of them mention it; but the latter mentions it as apocryphal, Legunt quidam et ad Laodicenses Epistolam, sed ab omnibus exploditur; "Some read an Epistle to the Laodiceans, but it is exploded by all." The seventh Ecumenic council, held in 787, states that the ancients allowed that there was an epistle with this direction, but that all the orthodox rejected it as supposititious. <div eID="gen51023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51024" type="x-p"/> An epistle ad Laodicenses is still extant in the Latin language, a very ancient copy of which is in the library Sancti Albani Andegavensis, St. Alban's of Anjou. Hutter has translated it into Greek, but his translation is of no authority. Calmet has published this epistle, with various readings from the above MS. I shall subjoin it at the end of this epistle, and give my opinion relative to its use and authenticity. A copy of this epistle stands in this place as a portion of Divine revelation in one of my own MSS. of the Vulgate.
entries.b6ee3fef0f647235fe579f520dfae2f35db2737b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen51024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51025" type="x-p"/> Say to Archippus - Who this person was we cannot tell; there have been various conjectures concerning him; some think he was bishop, or overseer of the Church at Colosse, in the absence of Epaphras. Whatever he was, it has been supposed that he had been remiss in discharging the duties of his office; and hence this direction of the apostle, which appears here in the light of a reprehension. But if the same person be meant as in the Epistle to Philemon, <reference osisRef="Plm.1.2">Plm 1:2</reference>, whom St. Paul calls his fellow laborer and fellow soldier, it cannot be supposed that any reproof is here intended; for, as the Epistle to the Colossians, and that to Philemon, were evidently written about the end of the year 62, Archippus could not be a fellow laborer and fellow soldier of the apostle at Rome, and yet a delinquent at Colosse at the same time. It is more likely, therefore, that the words of the apostle convey no censure, but are rather intended to stir him up to farther diligence, and to encourage him in the work, seeing he had so much false doctrine and so many false teachers to contend with.
entries.79dca0b6b5e303e15d17232a7b14cd598d86b6b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen51025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51026" type="x-p"/> The salutation by the hand of me Paul - The preceding part of the epistle was written by a scribe, from the mouth of the apostle: this, and what follows, was written by the hand of St. Paul himself. A similar distinction we find, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.21">1Cor 16:21</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="2Thes.3.17">2Thes 3:17</reference>; and this, it seems, was the means by which the apostle authenticated every epistle which he sent to the different Churches. The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle, so I write. <div eID="gen51026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51027" type="x-p"/> Remember my bonds - See what proof ye have of the truth of the Gospel; I am in bonds on this account; I suffer patiently, yea, exult in the Lord Jesus, so perfectly am I upheld by the grace of the Gospel. Remember my bonds, and take courage. How eloquent were these concluding words! That such a man should be in bonds for the Gospel, was the fullest proof of the truth of the Gospel. A cunningly devised fable could not have imposed on Saul of Tarsus; he was fully satisfied of the truth of the doctrines of Christianity; he proclaimed them as truths from heaven; and for their sake cheerfully suffered the loss of all things.
